<reason>PRO built a single clear route to victory—the state-sponsored or state-protected perpetrator whom no domestic tool can reach—and kept narrowing the debate onto it. CON's rigorous objections (recognition doesn't automatically confer jurisdiction; "wanton" embeds a contested harm-benefit valuation) were real but largely generic to every international crime, and PRO repeatedly made that point stick. Crucially, CON never named a tool that reaches a sitting head of state burning his own forest, and its Rebuttal 2 concession that alternatives only work once "a successor government" prosecutes was turned devastatingly in PRO's closing. CON's "which is it" permit dilemma was its sharpest moment and left some residual doubt about the boundary, but PRO's recklessness answer was adequate and CON's own "defensible domestically" concession blunted the vagueness line. Both sides used A1/A2 properly and avoided fake precision; PRO slightly overstated how automatically recognition binds third states. PRO made the debate easier to decide and framed the stakes more memorably.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 / Closing turning CON's [B4.1] "successor government" admission into "waiting for the perpetrator to lose," combined with pressing that CON's negotiated cross-border jurisdiction requires the same treaty-making it faults ecocide for—leaving CON with no tool for the protected incumbent.</best_rebuttal>
